chapter: WDSU radio and the New Orleans scene
title: First Black funeral parades and following the band
summary: He describes attending his first jazz funeral, a second in Algiers, the music, the exhaustion afterward, and the friendly strangers and musicians met along the route.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: I also, uh, well, let's see, only this year was I able to dig my first funeral. I don't mean my funeral, but I mean a colored funeral.
Yeah. Like, uh... Did you dig the graves?

No, I didn't dig them. I dig them. I dug the music, man. Mm-hmm. That was real crazy. I, uh, had been listening to you talk about colored funerals, and I'd heard about other people talk about colored funerals. And, of course, uh, I wanted to make one sooner or later. Mm-hmm. And one fine day, uh, let's see, where did we go? We went to, uh, Algiers. Way across... No, this one was over in, uh, uptown somewhere.
Gee, I'm trying to remember. Maybe at 8th and Daniel Street. That was, that's where I was.

The Elks Hall there. It used to be the Bulls. That was my first one, and I was surprised when I got there. There were artists with their sketching pads and pencils and pens and all kinds of people with cameras. And, uh, I just enjoyed it from beginning to the end. It was tremendous. And those dirages they play are indescribable. And, uh, although I've seen it written in magazines about those funerals, I, I still don't think it, they can be described. One has to see them from beginning to end to realize what they are. I mean, what a great big kid they are. The color is so much... It's... Undescribable. I, I went to a second one. I think the second one I went was in Algiers. Walked all day in the sun, hot, scorching sun. But I stuck with it. Right. And of course you were there, you were always at all of them.
Sun never seems to worry me too much, you know. Somehow the music's going.
When the music stops, you're exhausted.

Boy, I'll say. Then you notice all of a sudden. When it's all over, you realize. And you come to, and you realize how tired you are. And then there's that long trek home too. But you got something that stays with you for the next two or three days. And I find myself, after that, I find myself trying to persuade my friends to see one. I really do. And I said, you'll be sure to go see one. Because they're just wonderful. And they really are. In fact, when I go to Italy, I'm going to try and describe the Italian people. Those colored funerals. Because they're really. That's authentic New Orleans. If there ever was.
Well, who all did you meet as you walk along with them?

Well, you meet all kinds of people. Surprisingly enough, people which you've never seen before. All of a sudden, here you are talking to somebody you've never known before. And as you follow the parade. And sometimes it's just a lady who lives in the neighborhood. And she's lugging her child along with her, you know. Like little Sammy. I remember that time in Algiers. We lugged him. We took turns in carrying him. And of course, you meet the musicians too. And that's a great big thing. They always greet you and make you feel like you're the greatest person in the world. And actually, you're only coming there to listen and follow, you know. It's a real great thing.
They really treat you with respect, you know.
Mm-hmm. And they talk to you and want to know all about you. It's amazing.
